```{r compute}
# values quoted in the notes; same seeds and settings as the Wednesday R demos
# in CODE_Week9_MCMCAndStan.R
library(emdbook)
titer <- subset(MyxoTiter_sum, grade == 1)$titer
nll_gamma <- function(p) {
  if (any(p <= 0)) return(Inf)
  -sum(dgamma(titer, shape = p[1], scale = p[2], log = TRUE))
}
metropolis <- function(log_post, start, step_sd, n_steps) {
  chain <- matrix(NA, n_steps, length(start))
  current <- start
  lp_current <- log_post(current)
  for (i in seq_len(n_steps)) {
    proposal <- current + rnorm(length(start), 0, step_sd)
    lp_prop <- log_post(proposal)
    if (log(runif(1)) < lp_prop - lp_current) {
      current <- proposal
      lp_current <- lp_prop
    }
    chain[i, ] <- current
  }
  chain
}
set.seed(746)
keep <- metropolis(function(p) -nll_gamma(p), c(20, 0.05), c(4, 0.01), 20000)[-(1:2000), ]
ess_met <- coda::effectiveSize(keep)

rho <- 0.95
sigma_inv <- solve(matrix(c(1, rho, rho, 1), 2))
log_post_bvn <- function(p) -0.5 * drop(t(p) %*% sigma_inv %*% p)
grad_bvn <- function(p) -drop(sigma_inv %*% p)
hmc_step <- function(p, eps, L) {
  m <- rnorm(length(p))
  p_new <- p
  m_new <- m
  path <- matrix(p, nrow = 1)
  for (i in seq_len(L)) {
    m_new <- m_new + 0.5 * eps * grad_bvn(p_new)
    p_new <- p_new + eps * m_new
    m_new <- m_new + 0.5 * eps * grad_bvn(p_new)
    path <- rbind(path, p_new)
  }
  log_accept <- log_post_bvn(p_new) - 0.5 * sum(m_new^2) - log_post_bvn(p) + 0.5 * sum(m^2)
  list(p = if (log(runif(1)) < log_accept) p_new else p, path = path)
}
set.seed(3)
rw <- metropolis(log_post_bvn, c(-2, -2), 0.25, 200)
set.seed(3)
hm <- matrix(NA, 200, 2)
paths <- list()
p <- c(-2, -2)
for (i in 1:200) {
  s <- hmc_step(p, 0.1, 10)
  p <- s$p
  hm[i, ] <- p
  if (i <= 5) paths[[i]] <- s$path
}
ess_rw <- coda::effectiveSize(rw[, 1])
ess_hmc <- coda::effectiveSize(hm[, 1])

f2 <- function(v) formatC(v, format = "f", digits = 2)
f0 <- function(v) format(round(v), big.mark = ",")
```

```{r stan-fit, cache=TRUE}
library(cmdstanr)
myxo_code <- "
data {
  int<lower=0> N;
  vector<lower=0>[N] titer;
}
parameters {
  real<lower=0> shape;
  real<lower=0> scale;
}
model {
  titer ~ gamma(shape, 1 / scale);
}
"
t_compile <- system.time(myxo_model <- cmdstan_model(write_stan_file(myxo_code)))["elapsed"]
t_sample <- system.time(
  fit_stan <- myxo_model$sample(data = list(N = length(titer), titer = titer),
                                chains = 4, parallel_chains = 4, seed = 746,
                                refresh = 0, show_messages = FALSE)
)["elapsed"]
stan_summ <- fit_stan$summary(c("shape", "scale"))
draws <- fit_stan$draws(c("shape", "scale"), format = "draws_matrix")
n_div <- sum(fit_stan$diagnostic_summary()$num_divergent)
ci_stan <- quantile(draws[, "shape"], c(0.025, 0.975))
```

```{r sketch-helpers}
# scientific workflow schematic; 'highlight' shades one box (e.g. "FIT")
draw_workflow <- function(highlight = NULL, cex = 0.8) {
  boxes <- c("PROBLEM", "THEORIES", "MODELS", "FIT", "COMPARE")
  subs <- c("what do we\nneed to know?", "candidate\nexplanations",
            "data-generating\n(process + noise)", "confront each\nwith data",
            "fit, prediction,\nrelevance")
  x <- seq(1, 9, by = 2)
  y <- 2
  w <- 0.8
  h <- 0.55
  shade <- function(lab) if (!is.null(highlight) && lab == highlight) "grey80" else "white"
  par(mar = c(0, 0, 0, 0))
  plot(NA, xlim = c(0, 10), ylim = c(-0.2, 4), axes = FALSE, xlab = "", ylab = "")
  for (i in seq_along(boxes)) {
    rect(x[i] - w, y - h, x[i] + w, y + h, col = shade(boxes[i]), lwd = 1.5)
    text(x[i], y + 0.18, boxes[i], font = 2, cex = cex)
    text(x[i], y - 0.22, subs[i], cex = cex * 0.75)
  }
  arrows(x[-5] + w, y, x[-1] - w, y, length = 0.08, lwd = 1.5)
  rect(6 - 0.7, 3.2 - 0.35, 6 + 0.7, 3.2 + 0.35, col = shade("DATA"), lty = 2, lwd = 1.5)
  text(6, 3.28, "DATA", font = 2, cex = cex)
  text(6, 3.0, "study design", cex = cex * 0.75)
  arrows(x[3], y + h, 6 - 0.7, 3.2, length = 0.08, lty = 2, lwd = 1.2)
  arrows(6 + 0.7, 3.2, x[4], y + h, length = 0.08, lty = 2, lwd = 1.2)
  segments(x[5], y - h, x[5], 0.4, lwd = 1.5)
  segments(x[5], 0.4, x[1], 0.4, lwd = 1.5)
  arrows(x[c(1, 2)], 0.4, x[c(1, 2)], y - h, length = 0.08, lwd = 1.5)
  text(6, 0.15, "REVISE the problem and theories; drop or down-weight poor models",
       cex = cex * 0.85, font = 3)
}

# board reference: random walk vs. HMC on a narrow, tilted target
draw_rw_vs_hmc <- function() {
  g <- seq(-3, 3, length.out = 100)
  z <- outer(g, g, Vectorize(function(a, b) log_post_bvn(c(a, b))))
  par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(2.5, 2.5, 1.5, 0.5), mgp = c(1.4, 0.4, 0), cex = 0.8)
  for (k in 1:2) {
    contour(g, g, z, levels = c(-0.5, -2, -4.5), drawlabels = FALSE, col = "grey60",
            xlab = expression(theta[1]), ylab = expression(theta[2]),
            main = c("Random walk, 200 steps", "HMC, 200 steps")[k])
    if (k == 1) lines(rw, col = "steelblue") else {
      points(hm, pch = 16, cex = 0.4)
      for (pa in paths) lines(pa, col = "darkorange", lwd = 2)
    }
  }
}

# board reference: a puck sliding over the -log posterior "bowl"
draw_puck <- function() {
  par(mar = c(1.5, 1.5, 0.5, 0.5), mgp = c(0.5, 0, 0))
  curve(1.2 * (x - 5)^2 / 25 + 0.2, 0, 10, lwd = 2, xaxt = "n", yaxt = "n",
        xlab = "parameter", ylab = "-log posterior", ylim = c(0, 1.6))
  xs <- seq(2, 7.5, length.out = 40)
  lines(xs, 1.2 * (xs - 5)^2 / 25 + 0.28, col = "darkorange", lwd = 2, lty = 2)
  points(2, 1.2 * 9 / 25 + 0.28, pch = 19, cex = 1.4)
  arrows(2, 0.8, 3, 0.8, length = 0.08, lwd = 2)
  text(2.5, 0.9, "kick", cex = 0.8)
  points(7.5, 1.2 * 6.25 / 25 + 0.28, pch = 1, cex = 1.4)
  text(7.5, 0.75, "proposal", cex = 0.8)
}
```

# How to prepare (for students)

- **Big picture.** On Monday we turned simulated annealing into the
  Metropolis algorithm, and in Lab 7 you saw its weak spot: on a long,
  narrow, tilted posterior a random walk creeps, and you had to
  reparameterize by hand to fix it. Today: Hamiltonian Monte Carlo
  (HMC), the method behind **Stan**, which uses the *slope* of the
  posterior (the same gradient Newton's method used in Week 8) to make
  long, well-aimed moves. Stan is one of the most widely used tools for
  fitting custom Bayesian models in ecology, and we'll use it for the
  rest of the semester.
- **Read:** Monnahan, Thorson & Branch (2017), "Faster estimation of
  Bayesian models in ecology using Hamiltonian Monte Carlo," *Methods
  in Ecology and Evolution* 8: 339-348 (focus on the introduction and
  the comparison with JAGS; skim the details). Optional: Bolker 7.3.3
  (Gibbs sampling and BUGS, printed p. 315-319), and McElreath,
  *Statistical Rethinking* (2nd ed.), Ch. 9, for the friendliest
  picture of HMC.
- **Review:** Monday's Metropolis rule and the myxomatosis Gamma
  model; what a gradient is (Week 8).
- **Install Stan before Wednesday if you can** (the take-home WOD walks
  you through it): <https://mc-stan.org/cmdstanr/articles/cmdstanr.html>.

# Part 1: Lecture content

## 1. Big picture (~3 min) [BOARD]

```{r workflow-fig, fig.width=6.5, fig.height=2.6, dev="png", dpi=250}
draw_workflow("FIT")
```

- Point at **FIT**. Monday: Metropolis turns a posterior into samples
  without computing $P(y)$. Lab 7: it works, but on correlated or
  many-parameter posteriors it creeps, and you have to help it.
- Today: a sampler that uses the shape of the surface, and a tool
  (Stan) that builds it for you from a model description.

## 2. Why random walks struggle (~7 min) [BOARD $\to$ R]

**Board.** Sketch a long, narrow, tilted ellipse (Lab 7's raw-temperature
posterior). A random-walk proposal is a small circle around the current
point:

- Steps must be small enough to stay inside the *narrow* direction, so
  progress along the *long* direction is slow.
- A random walk covers distance only in proportion to $\sqrt{\text{steps}}$.
- With many parameters it gets worse: almost every random direction
  points "uphill."

**BUGS/JAGS (Gibbs sampling).** The first widely used tools (BUGS in
the 1990s; JAGS later) update one parameter at a time from its
conditional posterior. That works well when parameters are nearly
independent, but on a tilted ellipse it zigzags along the axes, with
the same slow progress.

**R demo.** Monday's myxo chain: 18,000 kept steps, but an effective
sample size of only about `r f0(ess_met[1])` independent draws for
shape. Then a correlated normal ($\rho = 0.95$): 200 random-walk steps,
effective size about `r f0(ess_rw)`.

## 3. Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (~10 min) [BOARD $\to$ R]

**Key idea.** Turn the $-\log$ posterior into a landscape and slide a
frictionless puck across it. The puck naturally follows the valley
instead of stumbling across it.

```{r puck-sketch, fig.width=4, fig.height=1.9}
draw_puck()
```

**Board, step by step.**

1. Give the puck a random **kick** (a momentum drawn from a normal).
2. Let it **slide** for $L$ small time steps of size $\epsilon$. Each
   step uses the **gradient** of the log posterior, so the puck speeds
   up going downhill and slows going uphill ("leapfrog" steps).
3. Where it stops is the **proposal**. Accept with the Metropolis rule
   on total energy; with small steps nearly everything is accepted.

- The gradient is what makes this work. Week 8 callback: Newton's
  method also used slopes, but to *find the bottom*; HMC uses them to
  *explore around* the bottom.
- Stan computes the gradient automatically from your model code
  (automatic differentiation): no calculus or finite differences.
- **NUTS** (the "No-U-Turn Sampler," Stan's default) tunes $\epsilon$
  during warmup and picks $L$ on the fly, stopping when the puck starts
  to turn back.

**Sticking point.** Students hear "physics" and assume HMC is a
different kind of inference. It isn't: it's still Metropolis
(propose, then accept or reject), with proposals that are far away and
still likely to be accepted.

**R demo** (skippable): the same 200 steps, random walk vs. HMC.

```{r rw-hmc, fig.width=6.5, fig.height=3, dev="png", dpi=200}
draw_rw_vs_hmc()
```

Effective size: random walk `r f0(ess_rw)`, HMC `r f0(ess_hmc)` out of
200. Each HMC step costs 10 gradient evaluations, and it's still far
ahead. (In testing, effective size swung a lot with $L$; that
sensitivity is why NUTS picks $L$ automatically.)

## 4. Stan: the myxo model (~12 min) [R]

**Walk through the model code** (in the script): three blocks.

- `data`: what's fixed (N, the titers).
- `parameters`: what's sampled, with constraints (`<lower=0>`).
- `model`: the likelihood (and priors; none here, so flat on the
  allowed range, matching Monday).

Every variable is declared with a type; lines end in `;`; comments use
`//`. Stan's `gamma()` takes shape and **rate**, so the code passes
`1 / scale`.

**Run it, then read the output.**

- 4 chains $\times$ 1,000 draws (after 1,000 warmup draws each).
- $\hat R$ (R-hat) = `r f2(max(stan_summ$rhat))`: the chains agree
  (want below about 1.01).
- Effective size: about `r f0(stan_summ$ess_bulk[1])` for shape from
  4,000 draws, vs. `r f0(ess_met[1])` from Monday's 18,000 Metropolis
  steps.
- Divergences: `r n_div`.
- 95% credible interval for shape: `r round(ci_stan[1])` to
  `r round(ci_stan[2])` (Monday's undersampled chain gave about 29 to
  81).
- Plot the draws on Monday's surface: they fill the banana.

**Cost.** Compiling took about `r round(t_compile)` s (once per model);
sampling about `r round(t_sample)` s.

## 5. When it fails; Stan vs. JAGS (~4 min) [BOARD]

- **Divergent transitions.** Where the surface curves sharply, the
  leapfrog steps overshoot and Stan flags a "divergence." Don't ignore
  them: the draws may be biased. Classic cause: the "funnel" in
  hierarchical models (returns in the multilevel weeks; the usual fix
  is reparameterization, as in Lab 7).
- **Discrete parameters.** Stan can't sample them (e.g. whether a site
  is truly occupied). You sum them out of the likelihood first, which
  is extra math. JAGS and NIMBLE handle these directly.
- **Multiple modes.** HMC still explores locally; well-separated
  valleys can trap it (run several chains from different starts).
- **Overhead.** Compiling, and a C++ toolchain to install. For a
  two-parameter model, anything works.
- Stan's payoff grows with the number of parameters and how correlated
  they are: multilevel models with hundreds of parameters.

## 6. Wrap, where to learn more (~2 min) [BOARD]

- **FIT**: grid $\to$ conjugacy $\to$ Metropolis $\to$ HMC. Same goal
  (the posterior), better engines.
- Learn more: Stan User's Guide and case studies (mc-stan.org);
  *Statistical Rethinking* Ch. 9; Betancourt (2017), "A Conceptual
  Introduction to Hamiltonian Monte Carlo" (arXiv:1701.02434);
  Monnahan et al. (2017); `brms` for regression models in Stan without
  writing Stan code.
- Hand out the take-home WOD.

## Discussion (~5 min) [BOARD]

> For the myxo model, Monday's Metropolis sampler took 20,000 steps
> (under a second) and gave about `r f0(ess_met[1])` effective draws
> for shape. Stan took about `r round(t_compile)` seconds to compile and
> `r round(t_sample)` seconds to sample, and gave about
> `r f0(stan_summ$ess_bulk[1])` effective draws from 4,000. A labmate
> says Stan is overkill: "my sampler was faster." Who's right? For
> your own research, when would you reach for Stan, and when might JAGS
> or a hand-written sampler be the better choice?

*Where to land.* Compare effective draws per second, not steps per
second; compiling happens once per model. For two parameters either
tool is fine. Stan earns its keep as models grow (many parameters,
strong correlations, hierarchical structure) and when diagnostics
matter. JAGS or NIMBLE can be easier when the model has discrete
latent states (occupancy, mark-recapture) that Stan would need
marginalized.

## 2. Why random walks struggle (~7 min) [BOARD $\to$ R]

- Sketch tilted ellipse; small circle proposals
- Steps limited by narrow direction; distance $\propto \sqrt{\text{steps}}$
- Many parameters: most directions go uphill
- BUGS/JAGS: Gibbs, one parameter at a time $\to$ zigzag

## 3. HMC (~10 min) [BOARD $\to$ R]

```{r podium-puck, fig.width=4, fig.height=1.9}
draw_puck()
```

1. Random **kick** (momentum)
2. **Slide** $L$ leapfrog steps using the **gradient**
3. **Accept/reject** on energy (almost always accept)

- Newton finds the bottom; HMC explores around it
- Autodiff: Stan gets gradients for free
- NUTS: tunes $\epsilon$, picks $L$
- **Still Metropolis**, with far-reaching proposals

## 4. Stan: myxo (~12 min) [R]

- Blocks: `data`, `parameters` (`<lower=0>`), `model`
- Types; `;`; `//`; gamma(shape, **rate**) $\to$ `1 / scale`
- 4 chains $\times$ 1,000; $\hat R$ = `r f2(max(stan_summ$rhat))`; divergences `r n_div`
- ESS shape `r f0(stan_summ$ess_bulk[1])` (vs. `r f0(ess_met[1])`)
- Shape 95%: `r round(ci_stan[1])`-`r round(ci_stan[2])` (Monday ~29-81)
- Plot draws on surface: fills the banana
- Compile ~`r round(t_compile)` s once; sample ~`r round(t_sample)` s

\newpage

## 5. Failures; vs. JAGS (~4 min) [BOARD]

- **Divergences**: sharp curvature; funnels; reparameterize
- **Discrete parameters**: marginalize (JAGS/NIMBLE direct)
- Multiple modes: several chains
- Overhead: compile, toolchain
- Payoff grows with \# parameters and correlation

## 6. Wrap (~2 min) [BOARD]

- Grid $\to$ conjugacy $\to$ Metropolis $\to$ HMC
- mc-stan.org; Rethinking Ch. 9; Betancourt 2017; Monnahan et al. 2017; brms
- **Hand out take-home WOD**

## Discussion (~5 min)

- Metropolis: <1 s, ESS `r f0(ess_met[1])`; Stan: `r round(t_compile)` s compile + `r round(t_sample)` s, ESS `r f0(stan_summ$ess_bulk[1])`
- "Overkill?" When Stan, when JAGS?
- ESS per second; compile once; payoff with size; discrete latent states $\to$ JAGS/NIMBLE
